headline: Ishraque Hossain to formally resign as State Minister for Liberation War Affairs today
summary: Ishraque stated on Facebook that he would make the announcement at 2:00 PM at the Jatiya Press Club, expressing his intent to work with renewed vigor as a BNP activist.
details: State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishraque Hossain is set to formally announce his resignation from the post today. The announcement will take place at 2:00 PM at the Jatiya Press Club.
In a post on his verified Facebook profile, Ishraque noted that some people were celebrating the news on social media. He acknowledged these reactions ahead of his official statement.

He further declared his intention to work against drugs with "100 times more enthusiasm." He specified that he would do so not as a member of parliament or state minister, but as an activist of the BNP.
caption:
State Minister Ishraque Hossain is set to announce his resignation today at 2:00 PM. He plans to refocus his efforts on combating drugs as a BNP activist.

State Minister for Liberation War Affairs Ishraque Hossain is set to formally announce his resignation from the post today. The announcement will take place at 2:00 PM at the Jatiya Press Club.

In a post on his verified Facebook profile, Ishraque noted that some people were celebrating the news on social media. He acknowledged these reactions ahead of his official statement.

He further declared his intention to work against drugs with "100 times more enthusiasm." He specified that he would do so not as a member of parliament or state minister, but as an activist of the BNP.

headline: Widespread exam fraud leaves job seekers distraught as merit is overshadowed by money in Bangladesh
summary: From exam cancellations to "center-contract" scams, a deep-rooted corruption network is undermining fair recruitment, forcing desperate candidates to pay millions for jobs. This systemic issue is crushing the hopes of countless young people.
details: In October, an exam for Assistant Upazila Youth Development Officer was postponed just minutes before it began, after question papers circulated on social media the night before. Millions of job seekers had traveled to Dhaka for the 242 vacant positions, only to face immediate disappointment. Despite a re-examination under special supervision, the incident raised serious questions about the integrity of government recruitment.

An investigation by the Special Response Battalion (SRB) uncovered a sophisticated ring involved in leaking questions and supplying answers. The leaked papers reached members of the ring hours before the exam, who then used fake WhatsApp IDs to distribute prepared answers to candidates. The ring allegedly demanded 8-10 lakh Taka for third-class positions and 15-20 lakh Taka for second-class posts.

The problem extends beyond question leaks to a new form of malpractice called "center-contract" fraud. This involves collusive arrangements between unscrupulous officials and exam centers to provide specific candidates with unfair advantages. Allegations include sending solutions via digital devices from outside the hall and silent support from invigilators inside.

Similar irregularities were reported during the recently concluded recruitment process for government primary school assistant teachers. In Nilphamari, serious allegations arose of answers being supplied from outside and special facilities provided in specific rooms shortly after the written exam began. Despite immediate protests from candidates, no visible administrative action was taken.

Such widespread fraud shatters the hopes of candidates who invest years of hard work and their families' savings into preparing for these exams. Ishrat Jahan Ira, a student from Begum Rokeya University, expressed her frustration, stating that news of question leaks or OMR sheet manipulation makes them feel like the sky has fallen. She emphasized that merit is being replaced by money.

The deep roots of question paper leaks and recruitment corruption are exemplified by the case of Syed Abed Ali, a former driver for the Public Service Commission (PSC). He and his associates allegedly operated a network of question paper leaks and recruitment fraud for years from within the constitutional institution.

Abed Ali's involvement first came to light in 2014 during a PSC recruitment exam, leading to a case where police found his direct involvement. Although judicial proceedings began in 2015, only two out of twelve witnesses have been presented in court over the past decade, highlighting a severe lack of accountability and prolonged impunity.

Taking advantage of this lack of prosecution, Abed Ali, his son, and several PSC officials and employees were re-arrested in 2024 on charges of leaking question papers for the Bangladesh Railway assistant engineer recruitment exam. Despite a chargesheet filed against 55 individuals after a lengthy investigation, the cycle of impunity continues due to unresolved previous cases.

Experts attribute the repeated failures in the recruitment process not merely to technological or individual corruption, but to institutional dishonesty and political considerations. They argue that the integrity of the system is compromised by these deeper systemic issues.

Professor Tanzim Uddin Khan of Dhaka University's International Relations department noted that exam committee responsibilities are often distributed based on political considerations when a political government is in power. He stressed that honesty and efficiency should be the sole criteria for committee members, a principle often disregarded in Bangladesh.
